new_entities.name: Fluoxetine for post-stroke motor recovery
aliases: fluoxetine after stroke for motor recovery
new_entities.description: Use of fluoxetine after stroke with the intention of improving neurological or motor recovery.

new_entities.name: Motor recovery
new_entities.description: Recovery of motor impairment and movement performance after neurological injury.

edges.effect_quant: A pooled analysis of 7,165 patients reported short-term improvement on NIHSS and Fugl-Meyer motor scores, but the large EFFECTS trial found no functional benefit at 6 months while increasing fractures and hyponatremia.
edges.population: adults treated in the acute or subacute period after stroke
edges.mechanism: Fluoxetine could plausibly support recovery by enhancing serotonergic plasticity and mood-related engagement in rehabilitation, but any motor benefit appears fragile and may not translate into meaningful independence gains. The main mechanistic concern is that a signal on impairment scales can coexist with no real-world functional advantage and more medication-related harm.
edges.summary: The strongest single trial in contemporary practice is EFFECTS, and it did not improve functional outcome after stroke despite earlier enthusiasm around fluoxetine-assisted recovery. Smaller trials and pooled analyses still suggest some motor-scale improvement, but the evidence is now too internally conflicted to call this reliably beneficial, so the right label is contested.
edges.caveats: This literature depends heavily on which endpoint is emphasized. Motor-impairment scales can show improvement while disability scales remain unchanged, and the larger pragmatic trials also raised safety concerns that make any marginal efficacy claim much less persuasive clinically.

evidence.notes: Recovery in Stroke Patients Treated With Fluoxetine Versus Placebo: A Pooled Analysis of 7,165 Patients.

evidence.citation: Lundstrom E et al 2020 Lancet Neurol
evidence.notes: Safety and efficacy of fluoxetine on functional recovery after acute stroke (EFFECTS): a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial.
